opus-5.5.text:
I think we're honestly still quite early. If you compare simulation to more established areas of machine learning, like image classification or language modeling, those fields have had years to converge on benchmarks and metrics that everyone agrees on. You train a model, you report accuracy on a held-out set, and people know how to interpret that number. Simulation of human behavior doesn't have that yet, and part of the reason is that the thing we're trying to measure is much harder to pin down.

When you simulate a person or a population, what does it mean to be "correct"? Human behavior is inherently noisy. If you ask the same person the same survey question two weeks apart, they won't always give the same answer. So one of the things we've tried to do in our work is ground the evaluation in that reality. Instead of asking whether the agent matches the person perfectly, we ask how well it predicts the person's responses relative to how well the person predicts themselves over time. That kind of normalization gives you a more honest ceiling, and I think ideas like that are the beginning of a more rigorous standard.

But I'd say we're in a phase similar to where social science itself was decades ago, where people are still debating what the right units of analysis are. Do you evaluate at the individual level, the group level, or the level of aggregate outcomes? Do you care about matching distributions, or about getting the right causal direction when you intervene? Those questions lead to very different metrics, and the field hasn't settled them.

What gives me optimism is that we can borrow a lot from disciplines that have thought about this for a long time: psychometrics, survey methodology, experimental economics. They have well-developed notions of reliability and validity. I think the maturation of simulation will come from combining those traditions with the scale and flexibility generative models give us, and from the community agreeing on shared datasets and evaluation protocols so results are comparable across groups. We're not there yet, but the pieces are starting to come together.

fable-5.1.text:
I think we're honestly still early. If you look at a field like statistics, there's a shared vocabulary for what it means for a result to be trustworthy. You have confidence intervals, you have p-values, you have well-understood notions of sampling error. Simulation, especially the kind of agent-based simulation that's now being powered by language models, doesn't have that yet. We don't have an agreed-upon way to say, "This simulation is accurate to within this margin, and here's the error bar on that claim."

Part of the reason is that the thing we're simulating is human behavior, and human behavior is messy and context-dependent in ways that resist clean formalization. When we built generative agents, the question we kept running into was, what does it even mean for a simulated person to be "correct"? Correct compared to what? One of the things I've tried to do in my work is to actually ground that in a measurable way, so, for example, taking real people, running them through surveys and behavioral experiments, and then asking how well the agent replicates those same individuals' responses. That gives you a number. It gives you something you can argue about and improve on. But that's one approach, and I wouldn't claim the community has converged on it as the standard.

The other challenge is that a lot of classical simulation, say in physics or epidemiology, has mechanistic models where the math is baked into the model itself. With language model agents, the "model" is this enormous, somewhat opaque system, and so a lot of the traditional tools for proving properties about your simulation just don't transfer cleanly. We're borrowing ideas from psychometrics, from social science replication work, from machine learning evaluation, and trying to stitch something together.

So my honest view is that we're in a phase that looks a lot like the early days of any empirical science. There are promising methods, there are early benchmarks, people are starting to care about validation instead of just demos. But if someone told me we have mature mathematical standards for simulation results, I'd push back. I'd say we have the beginnings of a methodology, and the next few years are going to be about turning that into something rigorous enough that a policymaker or a scientist could actually rely on it.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s still relatively early, especially when we’re talking about simulations of human behavior using generative AI. We can build systems that produce plausible behavior, but plausibility isn’t the same as validity. The harder question is: What evidence would let us trust a particular result?

I don’t think there’s going to be one mathematical standard that answers that for every simulation. You have to specify what you’re trying to model and what you’re going to use the result for. Can the simulation reproduce patterns in data that it hasn’t seen? How sensitive are the results to the assumptions you make? And can you characterize where it fails?

So I would distinguish the broader field of simulation, which has a long history of formal methods, from this newer effort to simulate people with language models. For the latter, I think establishing those validation practices is still a central research challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re still early, especially when it comes to simulations of human behavior. We can build a simulation that looks plausible, but that’s different from establishing that its results are valid for a particular purpose. We need to be clear about what we’re trying to reproduce, what evidence would validate it, and where the uncertainty comes from.

I don’t think there’s one mathematical standard that will settle all of that. A simulation might capture an aggregate pattern while getting individual behavior wrong, or work in one context and fail in another. So the important next step is to develop more rigorous ways of measuring those differences and defining the scope of the claims we can make.
